Around the world in 291 stops

Every Trip Sort level moves you along one real route. It starts in Montevideo, flies across every continent and ends in Stanley (Islas Malvinas). Here is the whole trip, stop by stop, on the game's own map.

The map

Follow the trip

The traveler goes round the route on its own, in the game's own toy plane. Drag and zoom the map, search for a city, or tap any stop to see its postcard.

The route starts in Montevideo (red pin) and ends in Stanley (Islas Malvinas) (gold pin). Gold pins mark where each chapter begins.

How you get there

290 flights between stops

After the twelfth level of a city, your toy plane flies you to the next one, across the game's own map. Tap to skip the flight whenever you like.

Collect them all

23 landmarks along the way

Reach a landmark's city and it joins your collection, with a short real story. Each one is also a Game Center achievement on iPhone.

Stop 6 · Rio de Janeiro

Christ the Redeemer

Christ the Redeemer has watched over Rio de Janeiro from the top of Corcovado mountain since 1931. The statue is 30 meters tall, its open arms span 28 meters, and its skin is a mosaic of thousands of small soapstone tiles. In 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

Stop 46 · Chichen Itza

Chichen Itza

The great pyramid of Chichen Itza, called El Castillo, is a calendar in stone: its four stairways of 91 steps plus the platform on top add up to 365, one for each day of the year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the setting sun draws a shadow serpent slithering down its northern stairs.

Stop 52 · New York

Statue of Liberty

A gift from the people of France, the Statue of Liberty crossed the Atlantic in 350 pieces and was unveiled in 1886. Her copper skin, no thicker than two coins, was shiny brown at first and slowly turned green over the following decades. Counting the pedestal, her torch rises 93 meters above the harbor.

Stop 69 · Tokyo

Mount Fuji

At 3,776 meters, Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, a volcano that last erupted in 1707. On clear days it can be seen from Tokyo, about 100 kilometers away, and every summer hundreds of thousands of people climb it to watch the sunrise from the top.

Stop 71 · Kyoto

Fushimi Inari Torii

Behind the shrine of Fushimi Inari, thousands of vermilion torii gates climb the wooded slope of Mount Inari, each one donated by a family or a business in thanks for good fortune. The path runs for about four kilometers, and the stone foxes along it are the messengers of Inari, the deity of rice and prosperity.

Stop 74 · Miyajima

Itsukushima Pagoda

Built in 1407 on a hill above the famous floating shrine of Miyajima, this vermilion pagoda rises 27 meters over the island. Its five roofs are covered in layers of cypress bark, and from its terrace you can see the great red torii gate standing in the sea.

Stop 82 · Beijing

Great Wall of China

The Great Wall of China is not one wall but many, built and rebuilt by different dynasties over some 2,000 years to guard the northern frontier. Counting all its branches it stretches more than 21,000 kilometers, and the best-preserved stretches near Beijing were built under the Ming dynasty, about 500 years ago.

Stop 93 · Siem Reap

Angkor Wat

Built in the 12th century for King Suryavarman II, Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five towers are shaped like lotus buds and stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and the whole temple is surrounded by a moat almost 200 meters wide.

Stop 105 · Sydney

Sydney Opera House

The sail-shaped roofs of the Sydney Opera House are covered in more than a million white and cream tiles that wash themselves clean when it rains. Its Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, won the design competition in 1957, and the building opened in 1973 after fourteen years of work.

Stop 109 · Uluru

Uluru

Uluru rises 348 meters above the flat red desert of central Australia, and much more of the rock lies hidden underground. It is sacred to the Anangu people, its traditional owners, and at sunrise and sunset its surface glows from orange to deep red.

Stop 125 · Agra

Taj Mahal

Emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and some 20,000 workers spent around twenty years finishing it. Its white marble is inlaid with precious stones and changes color with the light, looking pink at dawn, white at noon and golden under the moon.

Stop 152 · Dubai

Burj Khalifa

At 828 meters, the Burj Khalifa has been the tallest building in the world since it opened in 2010. Its shape was inspired by a desert flower, and it is so tall that the sun sets a few minutes later at the top than it does at its base.

Stop 157 · Petra

Treasury of Petra

The Treasury of Petra was carved straight out of a rose-colored cliff by the Nabataeans about 2,000 years ago, probably as the tomb of a king. Visitors reach it through the Siq, a narrow canyon more than a kilometer long, and its 40-meter facade appears suddenly at the very end.

Stop 162 · Istanbul

Hagia Sophia

Hagia Sophia was completed in the year 537 for the Byzantine emperor Justinian, and for almost a thousand years its great dome was the largest in the world. It has been a cathedral, a mosque and a museum, and its walls still show Christian mosaics beside Arabic calligraphy.

Stop 163 · Athens

Parthenon

The Parthenon was completed in 438 BC on the Acropolis of Athens as a temple to the goddess Athena. Its builders made the columns lean slightly inward and the floor curve gently upward, so that from a distance the whole temple would look perfectly straight.

Stop 186 · Moscow

Saint Basil's Cathedral

Ivan the Terrible ordered Saint Basil's Cathedral to celebrate a military victory in 1552, and it was finished in 1561. Under its colorful onion domes there is not one church but ten small ones, linked by narrow painted corridors. It stands at the edge of Red Square, in the heart of Moscow.

Stop 197 · Berlin

Brandenburg Gate

The Brandenburg Gate was completed in 1791, and the statue on top shows the goddess of victory driving a chariot pulled by four horses. For almost thirty years it stood right beside the Berlin Wall, and when the wall fell in 1989 it became the symbol of a reunited Germany.

Stop 202 · Paris

Eiffel Tower

Built of wrought iron for the 1889 World's Fair, the Eiffel Tower was only meant to stand for twenty years. At 330 meters it was the tallest structure in the world until 1930, and every seven years painters give its 18,000 iron parts a fresh coat by hand.

Stop 208 · Pisa

Leaning Tower of Pisa

The bell tower of Pisa's cathedral began to lean while it was still being built in the 12th century, because the soft ground beneath it gave way. Work stopped and started again over almost two centuries. Engineers have since straightened it a little, and today it leans about four degrees.

Stop 211 · Rome

Colosseum

Opened in the year 80, the Colosseum could seat around 50,000 spectators, who came to watch gladiators and wild animal hunts. A huge canvas awning shaded the crowd, and beneath the arena a maze of tunnels and lifts raised animals and scenery up onto the sand.

Stop 221 · London

Big Ben

Big Ben is really the name of the great bell inside the clock tower of the Palace of Westminster, renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012. The bell weighs more than 13 tonnes, and the clock is kept on time by adding or removing old penny coins on its pendulum.

Stop 230 · Giza

Great Pyramid

For nearly 4,000 years the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest building on Earth. It was raised for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago from more than two million stone blocks, and it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

Stop 232 · Aswan

Abu Simbel

Pharaoh Ramesses II had the great temple of Abu Simbel carved into a sandstone cliff more than 3,200 years ago, guarded by four statues of himself 20 meters tall. In the 1960s, to save it from the waters of a new dam, the whole temple was cut into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground.

FAQ

About the route

Where does the trip start and end?

It starts in Montevideo, Uruguay, goes round the whole world through 20 chapters and ends in Stanley (Islas Malvinas), back on the same side of the Atlantic, after 291 stops.

How many levels does each stop have?

Twelve. Each level paints a piece of the city's postcard; finish all twelve to complete it, stamp your passport and fly on to the next stop. That makes 3,492 levels in all.

Is the route the same for every player?

Yes. Stops unlock in order, so this map always shows where your trip goes next.

Are the places real?

Yes. Every stop is a real city, island or region at its real place on the map, and its tiles show what you would find there: food, animals, crafts and monuments.

What are the landmarks?

23 famous landmarks wait along the route, from the Eiffel Tower to the Great Wall. Reach their city to collect them, each with a short real story.
